text.p: Advertising agencies are facing increasing competition from management consultancies that are muscling in on their turf by providing clients with strategic branding and communications advice, industry experts say.
Graham Hinton, president of the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising and chairman of Bates Dorland ad agency, part of the Cordiant group, recently warned executives about the new competition.
"The threat of consultancies is very real for advertising agencies," he said at a seminar in London.
Management consultants are aggressively pursuing the growing business of advising companies on global branding and other areas linked to commercial communications.
Consultants recently told Reuters that the ad agencies that used to have a virtual monopoly on providing that kind of service had only themselves to blame for losing their grip.
Mike Sommers, who recently became a partner of Price Waterhouse, said many advertising agencies were providing too narrowly-defined a service for clients.

"Clients want creativity in the broadest sense, not just pretty pictures -- yet that is how advertising agencies continue to define their output," said Sommers, who is a lead partner in the newly-formed marketing and customer management division of Price Waterhouse.

"Ad agencies say, 'We can do what the management consultant is doing. Give us that job.' But they never offered to do it before," said Sommers, who used to be the marketing director for MGM Cinemas, TSB Bank and Woolworth Corp.
Management consultants such as McKinsey & Co are increasingly competing with ad agencies by providing advice on long-term strategic thinking, branding and winning market share.
"We are not telling clients that they need a new ad campaign or even a customer loyalty programme. We are helping companies reorganise themselves and identify areas for growth," Sommers told Reuters.
Several management consultancies have hired communications experts to help win business that might, in the past, have gone to ad agencies.
Management consultancies are enjoying explosive growth in the marketing and communications field in the United States and Britain, while growth is slower in mainland Europe, industry experts say.

The amount of money spent by companies in Britain on management consultants shot up from 28 million pounds ($46.5 million) in 1994 to nearly 80 million pounds last year, according to the Management Consultants Association.
It is a scenario that Martin Sorrell, chief executive of WPP Group Plc, has been warning about for some time.
"We face new competition from the established but ambitious management consultancies," he told advertising and design company executives late last year.
London-based WPP owns J. Walter Thompson, Ogilvy & Mather and about 40 other advertising- and marketing-related companies.

"There was once a time when client companies would welcome an agency's thoughts on just about all aspects of their business -- diversification, brand strategy, investment, internal training presentation, as well as advertising and promotions. All that has changed -- certainly in the US and the UK. Increasingly clients expect only creativity in their communications from their agencies -- and increasingly, that's all that agencies are organised to provide," he said.
The ad industry is also having to compete with management consultancies on a staffing level, since consultancies are attracting the best and brightest graduates into the profession.
Another problem for ad agencies is that in the past they have given away strategic advice for free when creating advertising campaigns, while management consultants charge fees for that service.
"If you get something for free, then you don't tend to value it as much as if you paid for it. It's all a matter of perception," said the chairman of one advertising agency.

Some ad agencies are fighting back against management consultancies by forming their own consultancy arms and offering client companies strategic advice from a higher level within the agency than was normally available.

Bartle Bogle Hegarty ad agency has launched BBH Futures which is advising clients such as Levi's and Audi, while Leo Burnett has formed the Brand Consultancy, Bates Dorland runs the Decision Shop and Euro RSCG Wnek Gosper has an "Upstream" division.
